overview: The Sri Abhaya Anjaneya Swamy Temple (Beechupally Hanuman Temple) is one of the most cherished Hanuman shrines in Telangana, nestled along the banks of the River Krishna, on NH-44 (formerly NH-7), in Beechupally village of Itikyala Mandal, Jogulamba Gadwal district — close to the Telangana–Karnataka border. Often called Dakshina Kashi and regarded as the 'Gateway to Srisailam', it draws thousands of devotees each year — particularly Srisailam padayatris and those performing asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan) at the adjacent Pushkar Ghat. Per temple tradition, the idol was installed ~200 years ago by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya; a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' (after whom the village is named) made daily offerings, and Lord Hanuman is locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'. The temple is revered as a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram where devotees seek strength, courage, freedom from fear, success in exams/jobs/court cases, and remedies for Shani and Kuja dosha. The idol, covered with a silver Kavach, is one of the few said to bear the 'Sanku Chakra' marks. A 1992-constructed Sri Rama temple stands nearby, and two islands (Gurram Gadda and Nizam Konda) dot the Krishna opposite the shrine.
summary: The Sri Abhaya Anjaneya Swamy Temple (Beechupally Hanuman Temple) on the banks of the Krishna River in Jogulamba Gadwal district, Telangana, is a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram popularly called Dakshina Kashi and the 'Gateway to Srisailam'. The idol was installed ~200 years ago by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya; the village is named after a young tribal devotee 'Beechupally'. Per tradition, Lord Hanuman is 'Sankata Mochana Anjaneya' (remover of troubles); devotees seek strength, courage, relief from fear and planetary doshas (Shani, Kuja), and blessings for exams/jobs/court cases. The adjoining Pushkar Ghat hosts holy dips, asthi visarjan (one-time fee ₹2,500 per the Brahmana Satram), and Pitr tarpanam. A 1992 Sri Rama temple stands nearby, and two islands (Gurram Gadda, Nizam Konda) lie in the Krishna opposite the shrine. Haritha Hotel Gadwal (~13 km) is the closest government-tourism stay, and the Beechupally Brahmana Nitya Annadana Trust provides food for pilgrims.

history.content: The temple is ~200 years old (per Hyderabad Zone, xploringdestinations). Per temple tradition, the idol of Lord Hanuman was installed by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the illustrious royal guru (rajaguru) of the Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya. After installing the idol, Vyasaraya left the area. That night, Lord Hanuman appeared in his dream and revealed that a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' had been making daily prayers to the idol — and so the village came to be called Beechupally, and the Lord is locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'. Originally, only the Valmiki community served as priests; later, Madhwa Brahmins (with the support of the Gadwal Rulers) were also allowed to perform rituals. The Gadwal Rulers conducted the annual religious chariot festival and supported the temple; this patronage continued as a tradition. In 1950, a road bridge across the Krishna was constructed (with a later NH-7 / now NH-44 highway passing through the village), opening up trade and transit from Rayalaseema to central India. In 1992, a large Sri Rama temple was constructed a little away from the river bank, housing several other deities. The temple sits on the banks of the Krishna River, ~30 km downstream of the Jurala Hydro Electric Project, with two islands (Gurram Gadda, Nizam Konda) opposite the shrine.

After installing, Vyasaraya left; that night, Lord Hanuman appeared in his dream and told him that a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' had been making daily prayers to the idol — the village is named after this boy.
Per Ramayana tradition, Lord Hanuman paused at Beechupally while carrying the Sanjeevani mountain to Lanka; prayers offered here are believed to go straight to Lord Rama through Hanuman.
The Hanuman idol is one of the few said to bear the 'Sanku Chakra' (conch and discus) marks, though the marks are covered by the silver Kavach.

sthala_puranam: Per temple tradition, Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya, installed the idol of Lord Hanuman here ~200 years ago. After installing, Vyasaraya left the area. That night, Lord Hanuman appeared in his dream and revealed that a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' had been making daily prayers to the idol — and so the village came to be called Beechupally, and the Lord is locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'. Originally, only the Valmiki community served as priests; later, Madhwa Brahmins (with the support of the Gadwal Rulers) were also allowed to perform rituals. The Gadwal Rulers conducted the annual religious chariot festival and supported the temple. Per Ramayana tradition, Lord Hanuman paused at Beechupally while carrying the Sanjeevani mountain to Lanka; prayers offered here are believed to go straight to Lord Rama through Hanuman, making Beechupally a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram. The riverside location also made it a natural and revered halt for pilgrims (including padayatra groups) travelling to the Srisailam Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga — hence its epithet 'Gateway to Srisailam' / 'Dakshina Kashi'.
religious_significance: Beechupally is a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram, popularly called Dakshina Kashi, and is regarded as the 'Gateway to Srisailam'. It is a significant stop for devotees on the way to the Srisailam Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga; many believe seeking Hanuman's blessings here before continuing to Srisailam makes the journey safer and obstacle-free. Padayatra (foot pilgrimage) groups traditionally rest and pray here, and the Pushkar Ghat is a major site for asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan) for families from Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.
spiritual_significance: Devotees believe Lord Hanuman here is highly responsive to heartfelt prayers, and that prayers offered reach Lord Rama through Hanuman. The deity is revered as 'Sankata Mochana Anjaneya' — the remover of troubles. The temple is sought for strength and courage, freedom from fear, success in exams/jobs/court cases, and relief from planetary doshas (particularly Shani and Kuja dosha). The deity is also believed to safeguard pilgrims during long journeys. Lockets of Sri Anjaneya are sold here and are considered powerful (per Tripadvisor visitor accounts).

architecture: The temple is built in the South Indian architectural style and is ~200 years old. The Garbhagriha (sanctum) houses a standing idol of Lord Hanuman covered with a silver Kavach, with the deity facing east and the temple facing south. Open mandapams invite the refreshing river breeze and natural light. A Siva Linga on the river bank gets wetted by the Krishna's waters during the peak monsoon. A 1992-constructed large Sri Rama temple stands a little away from the bank, with several other deities within the complex. The temple is on the banks of the Krishna River, ~30 km downstream of the Jurala Hydro Electric Project, on NH-44. The Pushkar Ghat adjacent to the temple has permanent bathing ghats built by the Telangana State government for Krishna Pushkaralu and asthi visarjan.

Celebrated with Yagnas and Poojas per the local festival calendar (per xploringdestinations).

The river festival held every 12 years, with holy dips, Pitr tarpanam and Asthi visarjan at the Pushkar Ghat. The Telangana State government has constructed many permanent ghats. The next Krishna Pushkaralu at this site is due in the 2030s.
Devotees, especially women and girls, light deepam near the large Dwaja Stambham; the surroundings are also filled with pleasant birdsong.

darshan_and_tickets.ticket_details: Sevas such as Abhishekam, Archana, Vada mala offering, and butter and sindoor seva are available at the temple counter (specific fees not published). Astikalu nimajjan (Asthi Visarjan) at the adjacent Beechupally Brahmana Nitya Annadana Trust building is a one-time fee of ₹2,500 (per a single Tripadvisor reviewer, Oct 2024), and dingi (small round boat) to the river for the immersion is ₹200–300. Annadana (food) is provided by the Brahmana Nitya Annadana Trust for pilgrims. Parking fee is collected at the entrance toll gate and at the river bank parking (per Tripadvisor).

accommodation.availability: The temple has 13 rooms (free of cost) for pilgrim accommodation. The Beechupally Brahmana Nitya Annadana Trust is the on-site accommodation/food provider. Haritha Hotel of the Telangana State Tourism Development Corporation (TSTDC), the closest government-tourism stay with good food and facilities, is in Gadwal (~13 km / per xploringdestinations, ~39 km per older sources).
accommodation.booking_process: Temple rooms are typically on a first-come, first-served basis; Haritha Hotel Gadwal can be booked via the TSTDC helpline 1800-425-46464 (per Mindtrip / xploringdestinations).

best_time_to_visit: Monsoon (July–September) for the spectacle of the Krishna at full flow and the river bank temple scenery; October to March for pleasant weather; Hanuman Jayanti (April–May) and Krishna Pushkaralu (every 12 years) are spiritually rich but crowded; Tuesdays, Saturdays and Amavasya are highly auspicious for Hanuman worship. Avoid stepping into other temples immediately after asthi visarjan (per Tripadvisor priest's advice).

travel.road: Located on NH-44 (formerly NH-7), on the Hyderabad–Kurnool highway, 200 m from the highway. ~150 km (per Tripadvisor plan41) / ~170 km (per nagesh5366) / ~200 km (per xploringdestinations) from Hyderabad. Common route: Hyderabad → Shadnagar → Kalwakurthy → Mahbubnagar → Gadwal → Beechupally. Regular TSRTC and KSRTC buses run from Hyderabad, Kurnool, Gadwal and Raichur. A road bridge constructed in 1950 across the Krishna connects the temple to the highway. The temple is 13 km from Gadwal Town.

top_reviews: Tripadvisor (plan41, 'BEECHUPALLI SRI ANJANEYASWAMY TEMPLE'): 'About 150 kilometres from Hyderabad, located alongside the National Highway 44 (formerly NH 7) by the bank of the Krishna River is an ancient and strikingly beautiful temple dedicated to Lord Sri Hanuman – the faithful Helper and Devotee of Lord Sri Rama of the Raamaayana lore. He is known here as Sri Aanjaneyaswami. The place is famously known as Beechupalli. There is a Hydro-electric Power Project named Juraala located about 30 kms from this shrine. A road bridge constructed across the River Krishna in 1950 has opened up a vital connection for trade and transit from Rayalaseema region as also from Southern India to the Central India via Telangana. The shrine is located about 200 metres away from the river bank where one finds a Siva Linga that gets wetted by the river waters during the peak monsoon period. A little away from the bank was constructed in 1992 a huge temple that was dedicated to Lord Sri Raama, although one finds several other deities within this complex. The shores of Krishna River at this location are noted for: (1) carrying out obsequies to the departed souls as per the Hindu Custom and (2) performing the ceremonial bath during the 12-year-cycle period of what is known as Pushkaram. A visit to this shrine is highly recommended to those who are facing difficulties in life. The Deity here is known to be very powerful in blessing the devotees in due fulfilment of all their earthly desires.' (5/5)

Tripadvisor (nagesh5366, 'Hyderabad to Beechupally for Astikalu nimajjan', Oct 2024): 'Beechupally Anjaneya Swamy temple is 200 meters from the Hyd - Kurnool highway. They collect a parking fee at the entrance toll gate and there is another parking fee at river bank parking. You can drive right from the temple entrance, a small single CC road and you will see the river and the bridge. There is a building to your right which has all the arrangements for astikalu nimajjan pooja and process. They charge a one time fee of Rs. 2500 and all the things needed are provided by them. They have stools for people that can't sit on the floor. 20 minute pooja and then you step out and go to the river. Generally people taking holy dips will not like you immersing astikalu near them so the best option is to rent a dingi (small round boat) to go into the river to do the nimajjan. They charge rs. 200 to 300 for the trip. Once done do not (as per my priest), enter any temples. Just go home. The cleaners will attack you for tips. They fight, curse, etc. Temple authorities and police seem to have failed in managing these people. The place is very very dirty...steps and access to Krishna river and the entire area is unhygienic and dirty. Once you are back on the highway based on your need and timing there are a couple of decent restaurants on your way back to Hyd. I started from Manikonda around 930 am and reached around 12. 20 pm. Left at 130 pm. Back home before 5. Distance is 170 kms from Hyd roughly, based on where you live in Hyd. The astikalu building seems to be open from morning to evening.' (3/5)

Tripadvisor (parusharouthud): 'The Anjaneya Temple is on the banks of river Krishna and is on the Highway from Hyderabad to Kurnool. The temple is very power full. On the day we saw many people taking Anjaneya Deeksha. The dwaja stambam is very big near which Women and girls are lighting Deepam in view of karthika masam being sacred month. The surroundinds and the temple premises are maintained well. Lockets of Sri Anjaneya are sold here which are said to be powerful. Only this Hanuman is known to have Sanku Chakra's which is no where found as per statements available on temple walls. However we cannot see it as Hanuman is covered with Silver Kavach. There is one more temple on banks of Krishna river which has Beautiful paintings. Very peaceful place to relax in the evenings. Surroundings were covered with pleasant noises of beautiful birds in the early mornings. Mind relaxing and stress free environment.' (5/5)

introduction.en: The Sri Abhaya Anjaneya Swamy Temple, popularly known as the Beechupally Hanuman Temple, is one of Telangana's most cherished Hanuman shrines, on the banks of the River Krishna in Itikyala Mandal, Jogulamba Gadwal district, beside the Hyderabad-Kurnool NH-44 highway. Often called Dakshina Kashi and the Gateway to Srisailam, it is a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram where Lord Hanuman is revered as Sankata Mochana Anjaneya — the remover of troubles. The ~200-year-old idol, installed by Sri Vyasaraya (royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya), is covered with a silver Kavach and is one of the few said to bear the unique Sanku Chakra marks. Devotees seek strength, courage, freedom from fear, success in exams/jobs/court cases, and remedies for Shani and Kuja dosha; the adjacent Pushkar Ghat hosts holy dips and asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan).

history.en: The temple is about 200 years old. Per tradition, Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya, installed the idol; a young tribal boy named Beechupally made daily prayers and gave the village its name. Originally only the Valmiki community served as priests; later Madhwa Brahmins, with the support of the Gadwal Rulers, were also allowed. The Gadwal Rulers conducted the annual religious chariot festival. A road bridge across the Krishna was built in 1950, and in 1992 a large Sri Rama temple was constructed nearby. Two islands — Gurram Gadda and Nizam Konda — lie in the Krishna opposite the shrine, ~30 km downstream of the Jurala Hydro Electric Project.

travel_guide.en: Beechupally is on NH-44, about 150 to 200 kilometres from Hyderabad (3.5 to 4.5 hours), connected by regular TSRTC and KSRTC buses. The nearest railway station is Gadwal, about 13 kilometres away, and the nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad, about 150 kilometres. The temple is open daily from around 6:00 AM to 8:30 PM (or 7:00 AM to 8:30 PM per Hyderabad Zone); the Astikalu nimajjan building is open morning to evening. October to March is the most pleasant weather; monsoon is spectacular for the Krishna scenery. The Beechupally Brahmana Nitya Annadana Trust runs 13 free pilgrim rooms and provides annadana.

faq.question: Where is Beechupally Hanuman Temple located?
faq.answer: In Beechupally (Beechupalli) village, Itikyala Mandal, Jogulamba Gadwal District, Telangana – 509125, on the banks of the River Krishna, beside NH-44 (formerly NH-7), 200 m from the highway. About 150–200 km from Hyderabad and ~30 km downstream of the Jurala Hydro Electric Project.

faq.question: Why is Beechupally Hanuman Temple famous?
faq.answer: It is renowned for its powerful idol of Lord Hanuman ('Sankata Mochana Anjaneya', remover of troubles) installed ~200 years ago by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya; the silver-Kavach-covered idol is one of the few said to bear the unique 'Sanku Chakra' marks. It is a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram, popularly called Dakshina Kashi and the 'Gateway to Srisailam', and a key stop for Srisailam padayatris and asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan) at the adjacent Pushkar Ghat.

faq.question: Is Beechupally called Dakshina Kashi?
faq.answer: Yes — Beechupally is often referred to as Dakshina Kashi because of its significant spiritual value for South Indian devotees, and as the 'Gateway to Srisailam' because Srisailam padayatris traditionally halt here to seek Hanuman's blessings before continuing to the Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga.

faq.question: What is the best time to visit Beechupally Hanuman Temple?
faq.answer: Monsoon (July–September) for the spectacle of the Krishna at full flow; October to March for pleasant weather; Hanuman Jayanti (April–May, Chaitra/Vaishakha) and Krishna Pushkaralu (every 12 years) are spiritually rich but crowded; Tuesdays, Saturdays and Amavasya are highly auspicious for Hanuman worship.

faq.question: What are the temple timings?
faq.answer: Per Hyderabad Zone and Mindtrip: 7:00 AM–8:30 PM daily. Xploring Destinations and the user doc give 6:00 AM–8:30 PM and 5:30 AM–1:00 PM and 4:00 PM–9:00 PM (with a short afternoon break) respectively. The Astikalu nimajjan building is open separately morning to evening. Treat 7:00 AM–8:30 PM as the most authoritative single source; confirm locally.

faq.question: Is Beechupally important for Srisailam yatra?
faq.answer: Yes — many devotees believe that visiting Beechupally Hanuman Temple before heading to Srisailam is key to a safe and successful pilgrimage. Srisailam padayatris traditionally halt and pray here; the temple is also the 'Gateway to Srisailam'.

faq.question: Are accommodation facilities available near the temple?
faq.answer: Yes — the Beechupally Brahmana Nitya Annadana Trust manages 13 temple rooms (free of cost, first-come, first-served). Haritha Hotel Gadwal (TSTDC, ~13 km) is the closest government-tourism stay with good food and facilities; booking via TSTDC helpline 1800-425-46464. More lodging is available in Gadwal town.

faq.question: Who installed the Hanuman idol?
faq.answer: Per temple tradition, Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja) — the illustrious royal guru (rajaguru) of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya — installed the idol of Lord Hanuman here ~200 years ago. After installing, Vyasaraya left; that night, Lord Hanuman appeared in his dream and told him that a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' had been making daily prayers to the idol — and the village came to be called Beechupally, with the Lord locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'.

faq.question: What is Astikalu nimajjan and how much does it cost?
faq.answer: Astikalu nimajjan is the ancestral ash-immersion ritual performed at the Beechupally Brahmana Satram building, adjacent to the temple. A 20-minute pooja is performed with all materials provided, then the ashes are immersed in the Krishna by dingi (small round boat, ₹200–300). One-time fee of ₹2,500 per a Tripadvisor reviewer (Oct 2024) — reconfirm on-site. The building is open morning to evening. Note: per the priest's advice cited by a Tripadvisor visitor, do not enter other temples immediately after asthi visarjan.

faq.question: What is special about the Hanuman idol?
faq.answer: Three unique features: (1) It is one of the few Hanuman idols said to bear the 'Sanku Chakra' (conch and discus) marks — though these are covered by the silver Kavach and not directly visible. (2) The idol is covered with a silver Kavach. (3) It is locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu' after the young tribal boy who gave the village its name through his daily prayers. Lockets of Sri Anjaneya are also sold at the temple and are considered powerful.
